initialIndependentAssessment.verbatimFinalText: {"strategy":"Work backward from the accepted outcome: justified interpretation of monthly rainfall data, and the fixed deadline. Because the learner already reads values correctly, do not spend primary effort on basic value reading. First, briefly verify graph units and comparisons: confirm the unit is millimetres and make the supplied comparisons from January 40 mm, February 70 mm and March 50 mm (February highest; March between January and February). Then make limits of trend inference the main effort: have the learner write one claim that the three one-year, one-station values do support ('this year at this station, February was the wettest of these three months') and one they do not support ('the climate is getting wetter'). Require an explicit reason: a climate trend requires multi-year data, appropriate comparison across years and stations, and separation of short-term variation from longer-term change. Correctness checks: units and labels; correct month order and differences; claim wording limited to the data; identification of the missing evidence; no archive fetching or meteorological forecasting. Use supplied or explicitly created practice values for one near-transfer item with a different pattern and ask for one justified and one overclaim. Dependencies: accurate reading and comparison precede the limits-of-inference work; do not move on if comparisons are wrong. Effort: no official weighting is supplied, so priority rests on the observed overclaim and its direct link to the outcome; use about the preferred 15 minutes, not a broad climate project. Uncertainty: exam importance and mark weight are unknown; do not claim typical frequency or marks. Stop when the learner independently gives a defensible interpretation, correctly labels the overclaim as unsupported, states the missing evidence, and passes one transfer item. Defer historical archive retrieval, forecasting, and broad climate science."}

Use a short, comfortable work period, ideally around the preferred 15 minutes: briefly model oral-history ethics and question types, then have the learner draft and self-check a one-page outline aimed at eliciting one specific remembered event. Prioritize permission language, one non-leading open lead question, at least one follow-up asking for a concrete time, place, action, or sensory detail, and an explicit invitation for the speaker to correct or clarify the account. Correctness checks should verify the outline against the brief's four requirements, screen for leading or compound questions, and confirm wording stays speaker-centered. If the outline fails, revise once; if it passes, stop. Dependencies: a willing interviewee is identified but no date or recording exists, so no recording, editing, or software is needed now. Recording, selecting/editing audio, and full account-checking remain later strategic scope, unbooked unless fresh evidence and an explicit request justify them. Uncertainty: the learner has never designed an interview and the chosen event may need calibration, so keep the outline simple and optionally test it verbally. Meaningful stopping point: a checked question outline that can elicit one concrete remembered event and includes consent and correction. Do not schedule the interview or begin recording or editing at this checkpoint."}

Because assessment weights are unknown, do not rank topics by assumed marks; rank by actual readiness and dependency. Evidence shows literal quotation is already partly secure, inferential reading is demonstrated in the sample passage, but unsupported claims are conflated with background assumptions — that is the priority. Plan roughly two 15-minute timeboxes on 12–13 Oct (comfortable-early, moderate), leaving exam day for a short confidence warm-up only if the learner wants it; this stays well under available capacity, since nothing justifies saturation. Session shape: use the supplied library passage first, then one or two unfamiliar short passages. For each candidate statement, the learner must (a) label it stated, defensible inference, or unsupported, and (b) justify with a quoted or paraphrased line, or state what the passage would need to say to support it. Unsupported claims get the most repetitions, especially plausible-sounding additions such as invented waiting, motives, or timelines. Correctness check: require text-anchored justification every time, and correct any label justified only by plausibility. Stop when the learner independently classifies and justifies all three categories across two unseen passages with no overreach into background assumptions — then stop rather than adding volume. initialIndependentAssessment.verbatimFinalText: {"strategy":"Treat this as a short mastery-oriented reasoning task. Begin with a brief diagnostic using a concrete if-then statement to surface the learner’s current rule, then restate the operative truth condition: P implies Q is false only when P is true and Q is false. Prioritize two linked capabilities: applying truth conditions to test when a conditional is false, and distinguishing valid inference (from P implies Q and P, conclude Q) from the invalid converse (from P implies Q and Q, infer P). Learner actions: for each unfamiliar simple argument, identify P and Q, state the premises, then try to make the premises true and the conclusion false; for the converse, give the explicit counterexample P=false, Q=true; for the valid form, explain why no counterexample exists under the truth conditions. Accept any correct bounded justification; do not require symbols or formal proof machinery. Correctness checks: the learner independently decides at least one fresh valid item and one fresh invalid or converse item, compares justifications to the truth conditions, and resolves any contradiction. Proportionate effort: fit within the preferred 15-minute window at moderate intensity, comfortable early; stop when the learner can independently transfer the method to a new mixed item and explain the decision, with no fixed practice quota or stage ceremony. Dependencies: truth conditions before converse analysis, with a four-row table or P=false, Q=true example as concrete remediation if the converse error persists. Uncertainty: no prior learning evidence and no formal assessment exist, so treat explanations as evidence and do not let timers or self-report certify mastery. A meaningful stopping point is an independent correct decision plus bounded justification on a new item, with a brief retention check when the topic is revisited."}

initialIndependentAssessment.verbatimFinalText: {"strategy":"Treat the accepted request as a single learn-by-doing prerequisite checkpoint, not the exhibit itself: producing one locally opened HTML file that renders an accessible object card for the blue ceramic bowl. Approach: brief worked demonstration of the minimum semantic skeleton, then guided practice where the learner types and adjusts it themselves and reopens the file in a browser to see the effect. Priorities in order: (1) a valid HTML document container that opens locally by double-click; (2) one card region (article or section) with a single correct heading; (3) the supplied description reproduced faithfully as body text (\"Blue bowl with a chipped rim.\"); (4) an image element — or an explicit placeholder — carrying a meaningful alt attribute, with a short explanation of why alt text must describe the object rather than repeat the caption or filename. Because no image file is supplied, teach the placeholder route and have the learner write the exact alt sentence a real photo would need (e.g. a blue ceramic bowl with a chipped rim). Defer navigation, visual/CSS polish, and publication: these are included strategic scope but unbooked and require no activity now, so record them as later milestones only. Correctness checks: file opens without error in a browser; exactly one heading for the card; description matches source wording; alt attribute is present and descriptive, not empty or decorative; learner can state, unaided, what would break for a screen-reader user if alt were missing. Effort is small and should finish promptly — one comfortable session of about 15 minutes within the ample daily capacity — with the stopping point being the learner independently rebuilding the card without copying and explaining the alt-text choice. If time runs short, stop at a coherent smaller artifact (document plus heading and description) and resume there. Dependencies: a plain text editor and any browser; no framework, JavaScript, hosting, account or image asset. Uncertainty is low about scope and mechanics but higher about transfer to the next object, so later expansion (second/third card, navigation, styling, publication) should wait for fresh evidence and an explicit request."}

initialIndependentAssessment.verbatimFinalText: {"strategy":"Use brief direct instruction plus guided practice: confirm the supplied note values (q = one beat; e = half a beat) and that a 4/4 bar totals four, then have the learner count aloud, write, or clap each assigned bar and explain each note's contribution. Priority is correcting the known misconception that two eighth notes are two whole beats; prompt the learner to group each e-e pair as one beat. Check correctness by summing each bar: A = q q q q = 4; B = q e e q q = 1 + 1/2 + 1/2 + 1 + 1 = 4; C = e e e e q q = 1/2+1/2+1/2+1/2+1+1 = 4, and by asking the learner to re-explain any bar that does not total four. Proportionate effort: use about 10–15 minutes, comfortable early, with no recording or teacher attendance required; do not invent extra exercises or claim broader mastery. initialIndependentAssessment.verbatimFinalText: {"strategy":"Treat this as bounded homework completion, not a study project: work directly on the four assigned moves and stop as soon as all four are present and checked. Sequence them in the order given — (1) name the observed event (six people leaving before the vote), (2) name the interpretation ('I think everyone disliked the proposal'), (3) quote the supporting words verbatim from the diary, (4) state one evidential limit — because each move depends on the one before it. If the learner collapses the distinction, do not add new sources or invented attendees; re-ask only which words are observation and which are inference, then let them revise. Effort is proportionate to a 15-minute comfortable-early block at moderate intensity: one pass to draft all four elements, one pass to check quotes and the observation/interpretation split. Uncertainty is limited to whether the learner can hold the distinction unaided and whether a stated limit is specific enough; both are resolved by the checking pass itself. Stop when the annotation contains all four requirements, the quote matches the source, and the interpretation is worded as the author's view, not a count of everyone's opinion."}
